section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) requires substantial graphics processing unit (GPU) memory.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: To design effective parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) workflows under tight hardware constraints, one must separate static parameter counts from dynamic memory allocations during backpropagation.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: In standard 16-bit fine-tuning with 32-bit Adam, total video random-access memory (VRAM) is divided across four main components: (1) static model parameters (2 bytes per parameter in FP16/BF16); (2) optimizer states, master weights, and gradients (16 bytes per trainable parameter in standard Adam); (3) forward activations retained for gradient computation; and (4) temporary workspace buffers for CUDA kernels and checkpointing.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: Early PEFT methods targeted parameter storage and optimizer state overhead by freezing the model backbone.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: Prefix-tuning keeps language model parameters frozen and optimizes a sequence of continuous task-specific vectors.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: By modifying only 0.1% of the parameters, prefix-tuning obtains comparable performance in the full data setting.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: Nevertheless, prefix-tuning maintains all pre-trained weights in uncompressed 16-bit precision and prepends continuous virtual tokens to every sequence, reducing effective input capacity and expanding attention activation memory.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: In contrast, BitFit freezes most of the transformer parameters and trains only the bias terms and the task-specific classification layer.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: BitFit modifies less than 0.1% of the total number of parameters.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: While eliminating projection optimizer states, its representational capacity is bounded since core linear projections remain fixed.

section: Introduction and Anatomy of Training Memory
text: Crucially, neither prefix-tuning nor BitFit compresses base weights.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) provides greater adaptation capacity while curbing optimizer memory by parameterizing weight updates as low-rank decompositions W = B A, where B Rd × r, A Rr × k, and rank r (d, k).
Because the base pre-trained weight W0 remains frozen, optimizer states and gradients are tracked solely for A and B.
Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times.

Importantly, this 3-fold memory reduction was measured specifically on GPT-3 175B under Adam optimizer partitioning; it does not transfer directly to smaller 7B models or long-context adaptation, where activation memory and base weights dominate total VRAM.
AdaLoRA parameterizes incremental updates in the form of singular value decomposition and prunes redundant singular values based on an importance metric.
Under a parameterized budget schedule, AdaLoRA always prefers allocating more budget to FFNs and top layers.
Dynamic pruning improves parameter efficiency but introduces scoring overhead during training.
Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation decomposes the pre-trained weight into magnitude and directional components and uses LoRA for directional updates.
DoRA reparameterizes weights as W = m V + V\|V + V\|c, with trainable magnitude m and low-rank V.
Detaching the normalization denominator from the backward graph prevents graph memory explosion.
The proposed gradient graph modification in DoRA leads to a training memory reduction of approximately 24.4% in fine-tuning LLaMA.
While LoRA and DoRA dramatically compress optimizer footprints, base parameters remain stored in 16-bit precision (~16 GB for an 8B model).
QLoRA overcomes this threshold by introducing 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization for frozen base weights.
QLoRA reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance.
To minimize quantization constants, Double Quantization saves an average of about 0.37 bits per parameter by quantizing the quantization constants.
QLoRA also introduces Paged Optimizers to manage memory spikes during checkpointing by paging states between GPU and CPU.
However, weights must be dynamically dequantized to BF16 during each forward and backward pass, increasing compute latency.
To avoid conflating architectural mechanisms with context-specific empirical outcomes, we separate structural properties from published experimental findings.

Methods with 16-bit base weights preserve maximum throughput and exact weight merging (W = W0 + W), but exceed 24 GB budgets beyond 8B models.
QLoRA eliminates this static ceiling but incurs runtime dequantization overhead.
We propose a controlled empirical benchmark on a single 24 GB GPU (RTX 3090 or RTX 4090).
Base Architecture: LLaMA-3-8B.
In 16-bit conditions (LoRA, DoRA), weights are loaded in native bfloat16 (~16 GB base VRAM).
In 4-bit conditions (QLoRA, QDoRA), weights are loaded in NF4 with Double Quantization via bitsandbytes (~5.5 GB base storage).
Compute precision is fixed to bfloat16 across all runs.
Adapter Configuration: Rank r = 16, = 32, adapter dropout 0.05, adapting all projection layers: query, key, value, output, gate, up, and down projections.
Batching and Sequence Grid: Micro-batch size B = 2 and gradient accumulation steps G = 8 (effective batch size 16), swept across sequence lengths L \512, 1024, 2048, 4096\.
Optimizer and Schedule: AdamW (1=0.9, 2=0.999), weight decay 0.0, 100-step warmup with cosine decay, learning rate 2 × 10-4.
Gradient checkpointing, FlashAttention-2, and seed 42 are fixed across all runs.
Warm-Up Iterations: The initial 10 steps of each run are discarded from measurement to eliminate CUDA context creation and autotuning transients.
Cache Clearing: Before each logged run, GPU memory is cleared using empty_cache() and reset_peak_memory_stats() in torch.cuda.
Peak Memory Profiling: Peak memory is monitored using torch.cuda peak allocation statistics, recorded separately at model loading, forward activation peak, and backward optimizer update.
Throughput Calculation: Throughput is timed over 100 steady-state steps with synchronized CUDA events (torch.cuda.Event), calculated as total processed tokens divided by elapsed time t.
Task Performance: 5-shot GSM8K test accuracy and validation loss.

An informal assertion was circulated within our research team: ``Our pilot halves training memory compared with LoRA.'' We explicitly emphasize that the statement ``Our pilot halves training memory compared with LoRA'' remains completely unverified.
No experimental code, hardware profiles, batch specifications, or measurement logs exist to substantiate this claim.
Therefore, it must not be treated as an empirical result or utilized as an assumption for the proposed study.

section: Scope and Limitations of the Literature
text: Reported memory savings often assume enterprise clusters or high-end accelerators (e.g., A100-80GB), leaving consumer GPU memory bus bottlenecks underexplored.
